title: kv-cache-offload-paging-design-draft-v3
content:
Status - Draft v3: consolidates kernel/paging experiments and adds concrete thresholds for PCIe vs UMA offload, plus scheduling hooks for batching and eviction. Primary author: Ayesha Patel. Reviewers: Ben, Maria, Ethan, Priya.

Purpose and scope: This doc captures proposed designs and heuristics for KV cache offload and host-memory paging in the Redwood serving runtime. Goals: reduce GPU memory OOMs for long-context workloads, maintain low tail latency, and keep per-token cost reasonable. We cover: offload media (host DRAM over PCIe vs shared-UMA), kernel-level choices (pinned pages, hugepages, async DMA), paging/eviction policies, scheduling hooks to avoid GPU stalls, instrumentation, and rollout plan.

Motivation: Large context LLMs create huge KV caches (per-layer KV for many tokens). On memory-constrained GPUs this leads to either lower max context or OOMs. Naive spilling to host memory (page fault driven, swap-like) causes unpredictable tail latency and GPU stalls. We need deterministic, measurable offload behavior integrated with batching/scheduling to ensure latency SLOs.

Key constraints and assumptions: Target HW: cloud VMs with discrete GPUs (PCIe Gen3/Gen4/Gen5) and instances with UMA (e.g., APU-like or integrated) are considered separately. Host DRAM bandwidth and PCIe bandwidth are orders of magnitude lower than device-local HBM for small random accesses; sequential DMA transfers approach higher throughput. Typical KV access pattern: high temporal locality for recent tokens, but long-tail random-access when decoding long prompts or when serving many concurrent contexts. Serving runtime must support both hosted API and Dedicated deployments; design must be configurable per-customer.

Design overview: We propose a tiered KV storage model: (1) On-device HBM (fastest, primary). (2) Pinned host DRAM (or numa-local DRAM) accessible via explicit DMA over PCIe (medium latency, predictable). (3) NVMe-backed on-host swap as a last resort for very cold entries (background prefetch/evict only).

Operational modes by platform: Discrete GPU (PCIe): prefer explicit offload to pinned host DRAM via async DMA. Use batching of DMA transfers and prefetch heuristics to avoid per-token DMA on the critical path. UMA or integrated memory: use memory mappings that allow direct device access; still treat non-local pages as slower tier and keep similar eviction heuristics.

Offload interface and kernel-level considerations: Pinned pages: allocate pinned host pages for KV slabs to ensure stable physical addresses for DMA. Use madvise/MLOCK to reduce page faults. Hugepages: when per-entry size is large, use 2MB hugepages to reduce TLB pressure (helps for UMA and CPU-side scanning). Experimental flag for enabling hugepages for pinned regions. DMA engine and async transfers: use a runtime DMA queue per device to schedule offload/fetch ops. DMA ops are batched per-request-window to improve PCIe utilization. Memory registration: maintain a registration cache to avoid re-registering host memory for repeated offload. Fallback for page faults: do NOT rely on kernel page-fault semantics for correctness on the fast path; page faults lead to stalls. Put a guard where any fault on a pinned region triggers an immediate retry path that blocks scheduling until DMA completes (measured and limited).

Paging and eviction policies: We need a hybrid policy that balances hit-rate and DMA cost. Proposed policy parameters (tunable): GPU-resident high watermark (HW): fraction of device KV capacity where we start to consider offload. default 0.82 (82%). GPU-resident low watermark (LW): fraction to reclaim down to after offload. default 0.65 (65%). Host-resident soft cap: cap on pinned host RAM used for cold entries per-device. default 1.5x device HBM size, configurable per-deployment. Entry eviction score: composite of recency (LRU timestamp), frequency (access count), and cost-to-fetch (bytes * estimated PCIe latency). Cold vs warm threshold: entries not accessed in N tokens (default N=2048) are cold candidates. Prefetch window: when decoding with high locality (recent tokens), prefetch next K layers/kv segments into device HBM ahead of usage. default K=2 segments.

Eviction algorithm (simplified): (1) When device HBM usage > HW, mark entries for offload until usage <= LW. (2) Select entries with lowest eviction score, prefer bulk-contiguous slabs to enable large DMA. (3) Schedule batched DMA out to pinned host DRAM. Do not evict entries currently referenced by active batches or streaming outputs. (4) Maintain a per-stream working set to avoid evicting items needed by active decoding requests.

Prefetch heuristics and scheduling hooks: Scheduler integrates with batching: when a decoding batch is formed, runtime computes the union of KV keys required for the next M tokens for each stream and ensures those entries are device-resident or enqueued for prefetch. DMA transfers invoked as non-blocking prefetchs; if prefetch misses the deadline (still in flight at token decode time) fall back to a slower decode path using host-resident access with careful pacing to avoid GPU stalls. Backpressure: if DMA queue depth exceeds a threshold or PCIe bandwidth is saturated, the scheduler temporarily reduces max batch size and raises priority for streams with stricter latency SLOs.

UMA-specific notes: UMA systems can avoid DMA but still exhibit higher access latency for non-local pages. Treat UMA cold pages as host-tier but use normal loads/stores with awareness of cache coherency costs. Use NUMA-aware allocation and prefer memory on the same NUMA node as the GPU PCI root if possible.

Performance/latency tradeoffs and thresholds: We propose the following conservative defaults; they must be validated in perf runs per instance type: HW (start offload): 82% GPU HBM utilization. LW (stop offload): 65% GPU HBM utilization. Max concurrent DMA throughput cap per device: 0.6 * measured PCIe sustained bandwidth (to leave headroom). DMA batch size: aim for 4MB-32MB transfers; smaller transfers (<256KB) are inefficient on PCIe and should be avoided unless necessary. Max DMA inflight ops default: 8. Tunable per device.

Kernel/OS tuning recommendations: Ensure mlock limits are sufficient for pinned regions (increase RLIMIT_MEMLOCK for the runtime process). Enable hugetlbfs or transparent hugepages for large pinned allocations where latency is critical. Test both modes. Avoid kernel swap for pinned regions; mark pages with MLOCK to prevent swapping. Monitor /proc/slabinfo and device driver pinned allocations to avoid fragmentation.

Instrumentation and observability: Track the following metrics per-device and per-host: KV hit rate (device vs host vs Nvme). Average and p99 fetch latency for host->device DMA and device->host writes. PCIe bandwidth utilization and DMA queue depth. GPU stall time attributable to waiting on KV fetches. Eviction rate and re-fetch rate (how often evicted entries are brought back). Cost estimate delta (tokens/sec per-dollar) when enabling offload.

Safety, rollout, and config knobs: Default to disabled for existing customers; enable behind a runtime flag and feature gate. Start with non-critical workloads and measure tail latency impact. Provide two modes: aggressive (maximizes capacity, tolerates higher p99) and conservative (preserves p99 at expense of capacity). Allow per-customer overrides for HW/LW and max pinned host RAM.

Open questions and experiments planned: (1) Optimal HW/LW settings per model and per-device class. Plan: run grid sweep across HW in {0.7,0.8,0.85,0.9} and LW in {0.5,0.6,0.7} while measuring throughput and p99. (2) Effectiveness of hugepages for pinned regions in reducing p99. Plan: microbench DMA latency tests and end-to-end decode p99. (3) Prefetch depth K and its effect on extra DMA bandwidth vs p99. Characterize diminishing returns. (4) NVMe-as-tier: evaluate throughput and cost-per-token for very cold workloads; likely useful only for batched background writes and extremely high context lengths. (5) UMA behavior: benchmark on representative UMA instances and compare to PCIe cases.

Implementation milestones: Spike A (2w): DMA pipeline and pinned allocation primitives; simple offload/restore for contiguous KV slabs. Spike B (2w): Scheduler integration prototype: prefetch for a single model and measure p99 with synthetic workloads. Beta (6w): Full eviction policy, heuristics, observability, and flags. Deploy to staging. Canary (4w): Gradual rollouts to small percentage of production traffic with conservative defaults. GA (TBD): After stability and perf validation.

Appendix: quick checklist for infra and SRE: Monitor PCIe errors and DMA timeouts; implement auto-retry and alerting. Add autoscaler awareness: when device HBM pressure is consistently high, consider scaling out rather than over-aggressively offloading. Add billing instrumentation for host RAM used by pinned regions per-customer.

References and related docs: Previous drafts: kv-cache-offload-paging-design-draft.json, kv-cache-offload-paging-design-draft-v2.json (see linked_artifacts). Kernel notes: pinned memory semantics, mlock docs, hugetlbfs. Perf measurements: pending; schedule measurement runs on p4d / a2 / g5 instances.

Notes to reviewers: Focus reviewer attention on eviction scoring formula and HW/LW defaults. We need to align on rollback behavior: prefer conservative defaults to minimize p99 regressions.
